content.thinking:
I'm checking whether the root-cause claim holds: turning off the legacy fallback routed account pages to the new renderer, and whether those pages hit the spend-per-item figure. The sources support the first part, but the link to that figure still reads as hedged, so I need to see how firmly it's stated.

I'm checking the remaining claims: the spend-per-item function divides this month's total by this month's purchase count with no guard for empty input, and the cause is described as a likely break rather than a confirmed one. The "would fail" prediction about turning the flag back on is a what-if, so I'm only going to count what the sources say actually happened.

I'm checking the causal chain against the timestamps: the flag went off at 01:58, pages failed through the window that ended at 02:05, and the ZeroDivisionError lines up with that same range. Each claim there has a source behind it, though I still need to confirm the "typically 0" detail for the new renderer.

I'm checking the remaining causal links now. The flag was switched off at 01:58:33, the same moment the new renderer's error rate jumped, and turning it back off left the incident at its level until it was put back on. The open question is whether pages served by the new renderer actually reach the spend function, since the sources only confirm that the function divides by zero and that the new renderer raises the error.

I'm confirming the contributing factors: no check on the new renderer path was seen, and the existing tests don't cover this shopper there. The flag change pushed all account-page traffic to the new renderer at essentially the same moment, and from the minute after the switch every evaluation read off.

I'm checking the contributing factors now: the flag change moved all account-page traffic at once, with no staged rollout or automatic halt, and the error itself named the spend-summary code, which made the cause harder to see.

I'm going back over the remaining support for the root cause: the fallback flag, the new renderer's error count at onset, and the spend-summary function. Those points check out against the record, and the label "root cause" still holds. Still, I'm treating the "would fail" warning and the reversion ordering as things I'll only credit as far as what happened.

I'm confirming the error-rate figure at 02:02 against the logs, and it checks out, so the causal chain stands as written.

supported.quote: Switching legacy-checkout-fallback off sent account pages to the new renderer, and those pages reach average_spend_per_item_this_month in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py.
Code-Fix read that function as dividing this month's spend total by the number of purchases made this month, with nothing to handle a month with no purchases.

So for any shopper who has bought before but not this month, the division raises ZeroDivisionError and the account page fails. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.

Someone turned off a setting that kept account pages on their older version, which sent shoppers to a newer version that likely breaks when it works out an average of this month's spending for anyone who has bought nothing this month.
If legacy-checkout-fallback is switched off again, the new renderer would serve account pages again, and they would fail for shoppers who have bought nothing this month.
Shoppers' account pages failed to load

It did not change what was done: the lead was weighed as unverified, monthly-spend-feature was reverted first, and the flag it named was turned back on only after that revert was refuted, as the Investigator's second candidate.
Shoppers' account pages failed: account page requests came back as failed pages, and the logged account-page error rate peaked at {Gbac1.7}.
Account page requests raised a ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.1} of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py over {G5309.3}, and each request that raised it failed.

At {P1.1} the flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off, and account pages moved from the legacy renderer to the new one. At {G7ad6.6}, {G7ad6.1} of the flag's evaluations read off. Over {G7037.4} every evaluation read off. The new renderer's count of account pages served was highest at {Gc27d.11}, after being typically {Gc27d.10} before.
The switch-on of monthly-spend-feature at {P2.1}, made at the same instant (candidate C1). Turning that flag back off left the service at the incident's level, so the flag was put back on.

Pages served by the new renderer reach average_spend_per_item_this_month, which, as Code-Fix reads it, divides by the number of purchases made this month and so fails for any shopper who has bought nothing this month.
Before legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off in production, no check was seen that the new renderer serves an account with past purchases but none this month.

The flag change moved all account-page traffic to the new renderer at once. Every evaluation read off from the minute after the switch, and no staged rollout or automatic halt on rising errors was seen.

legacy-checkout-fallback and monthly-spend-feature were changed by the same admin at the same instant, and the error named the spend-summary code. That made it hard to tell which change caused the failures.
Nobody was paged. No on-call incident was linked to the alert, so no person was called in to work it.
rows: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one

supported.quote: The investigation ranked monthly-spend-feature above legacy-checkout-fallback because the error named the spend-summary code, so the first revert went to the wrong flag. Yet the new renderer's count at the onset matched the fallback flag's off evaluations, and the thread had named the fallback flag.
